newsitem.title: THAILAND: Clinton heads to Thailand to strengthen trade ties.
newsitem.headline: Clinton heads to Thailand to strengthen trade ties.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton arrives in Bangkok late on Monday for a brief state visit to commemorate the Thai king's 50th anniversary on the throne and to strengthen commercial ties, diplomats and analysts said.
Clinton's visit as a guest of King Bhumibol Adulyadej, the world's longest-reigning monarch, marks the first U.S. presidential visit to Thailand in 27 years.
Thai diplomats and analysts said Clinton's 27-hour visit to Bangkok was intended to show America's interest in Asia and help boost trade and commercial ties with Thailand.

"His long-awaited trip will not only strengthen Thai-U.S. relations, which are based on the shared values of democracy and freedom, but also reaffirm the U.S.'s strong commitment to peace and security in Southeast Asia," an editorial in the Nation newspaper said on Monday.
Thailand's people are expected to offer a warm welcome to Clinton, due in part to the fact that their beloved King Bhumibol was born in the United States.

But preparations haven't been snag-free. American and Thai flags set up along the route Clinton will travel have been disappearing and officials have been posted to stand watch to prevent any further flag-pilfering.
Clinton's visit to Bangkok is the last leg of his first overseas trip since being re-elected earlier this month. He arrives from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in the Philippines.
Diplomats say a presidential visit -- the last was in 1969 by Richard Nixon during the Vietnam War -- is a good opportunity to boost commercial ties.

Although Thailand's economy has slowed this year, the World Bank ranked it as the fastest-growing economy in the world during the past decade and offers good opportunities for American companies, a U.S. official said.
Two-way trade amounts to about $18 billion, with Thailand enjoying a trade surplus with the United States, its biggest single export market.
Economic analysts hope a tax treaty to be signed by Clinton and Thai officials during the visit will help boost trade.

The treaty, which took more than a decade of negotiation to hammer out, eliminates double taxation on the earnings of U.S. firms operating in Thailand and vice versa, with the goal of encouraging more investment and technology transfer between the two countries.
Clinton is due to hold talks with the Thai premier on economic and security issues as well as drug trafficking, which remains rampant in Thailand and neighbouring countries.
He may also be the first head of state to meet Thailand's next prime minister, Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, who is expected to be officially named to the post shortly before Clinton arrives.

Clinton's visit has sparked an effort to speed up the process of installing New Aspiration Party (NAP) leader Chavalit to replace Premier Banharn Silpa-archa of the Chart Thai party so that Clinton won't have to meet with a lame duck leader.
Chavalit's NAP won a slim victory in a November 17 election. It normally takes about two weeks after an election before a new premier is sworn in.

Clinton is scheduled to give a speech at Bangkok's Chulalongkorn University on Tuesday afternoon. He and First Lady Hillary Clinton, who was on a separate visit to northern Thailand on Sunday and Monday, will leave for the United States at about midnight on Tuesday.
